newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Japan game makers launch legal war on HK pirates.
newsitem.headline: Japan game makers launch legal war on HK pirates.

text.p: Three Japanese electronics giants declared war on computer game copyright pirates Thursday by launching an unusual joint legal action against Hong Kong distributors and retailers of counterfeited software.

Sega Enterprises Ltd., Koei Co. Ltd. and Sony Corp.'s Sony Computer Entertainment Inc. said they had fired off a volley of writs against 43 distributors and retailers, seeking injunctions and compensation for trademark and copyright violations.

Kiichi Nishikura, general counsel for Sega, said software pirates were banding together into a loose syndicate in Hong Kong as well as Taiwan, China, Southeast Asia, and South American nations such as Paraguay.
"Therefore manufacturers for software developing companies have to be united also," Nishikura told a news conference.
"This is the beginning. I think Nintendo (Co. Ltd.) will also participate in the near future. We must control these counterfeiting activities, otherwise our companies will go bankrupt," he said.
Nishikura estimated 90 percent of game software sold in Hong Kong was pirated, selling for one-tenth the price of legitimate products. He declined to estimate the size of the market.
More writs would be filed in the future as more evidence was gathered, he added.
Shih Yann Loo of law firm Baker & McKenzie, which is handling the cases, said investigators had purchased software in the stores named in the writs and secretly videotaped the transactions.
Photographs of the store employees handling the transactions were stapled to the writs, forcing the businesses to take seriously the usually difficult-to-prove complaints, he said.
Nishikura acknowledged that hitting retailers was only scratching the surface but said manufacturers had to start somewhere.
The electronics firms were also cooperating with various authorities to gather evidence that have led to recent raids of factories in China, Taiwan and Paraguay, he said.
Nishikura said Beijing was taking the piracy problem very seriously, but noted local enforcement was at times difficult.

Copyright violation in China is a major problem for many multinational companies, but Beijing has vowed to clamp down on pirates and open its cultural markets in a June agreement with the United States that narrowly averted a multi-billion dollar trade war between the two countries.

Nishikura said Hong Kong, a major conduit for China's pirated products, was a major centre of the counterfeiting industry, but noted the problem was found in other centres such as Singapore and the United Arab Emirates' Dubai.
Pirates in different countries were working more closely together, he said. "They have connections," he said.
